metadata.title: Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture

extraction_notes.note: proof or remark: the two sentences after Cauchy's Interlace Theorem justify it only by pointing to the Courant-Fischer-Weyl principle and to Fisk; kept as an origin-external proof so the imported result shows where its proof lives.
example or external theorem: the cited AND-of-ORs tightness for Theorem 1.4 is one sentence without a formula; kept as an example illustrating TP8.
Theorem 1.1's tightness clause has no proof in the paper; it rests on the Chung-Furedi-Graham-Seymour construction quoted in the introduction, so it is a nested claim fed by TP2.
'This confirms a conjecture of Gotsman and Linial' names a conjecture the paper never states, so it has no node; Virza's construction is only mentioned and has none either.

nodes.name: Hypercube graph $Q^n$
nodes.statement: Let $Q^n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph, whose vertex set consists of vectors in $\{0, 1\}^n$, and two vectors are adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate.
differentia: whose vertex set consists of vectors in $\{0, 1\}^n$
two vectors are adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate
also_stated_at: Recall that $Q^n$ denotes the $n$-dimensional cube graph.

nodes.name: Maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ and largest adjacency eigenvalue $\lambda_1(G)$
nodes.statement: For an undirected graph $G$, we use the standard graph-theoretic notations $\Delta(G)$ for its maximum degree, and $\lambda_1(G)$ for the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix.

nodes.name: Chung-Füredi-Graham-Seymour logarithmic lower bound
nodes.statement: In 1988, Chung, F\"uredi, Graham, and Seymour \cite{cfgs_cube} proved that if $H$ is an induced subgraph of more than $2^{n-1}$ vertices of $Q^n$, then the maximum degree of $H$ is at least $(1/2-o(1)) \log_2 n$.
assumptions: $H$ is an induced subgraph of more than $2^{n-1}$ vertices of $Q^n$
conclusions: the maximum degree of $H$ is at least $(1/2-o(1)) \log_2 n$
nodes.statement_short: Every induced subgraph of $Q^n$ on more than $2^{n-1}$ vertices has maximum degree $\ge (1/2-o(1))\log_2 n$.

nodes.name: Chung-Füredi-Graham-Seymour construction
nodes.statement: Moreover, they constructed a $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph whose maximum degree is $\lceil \sqrt{n}\, \rceil$.
conclusions: they constructed a $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph whose maximum degree is $\lceil \sqrt{n}\, \rceil$
nodes.statement_short: There is a $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph of $Q^n$ with maximum degree $\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$.

nodes.name: Even vertices of $Q^n$ are independent
nodes.statement: Note that the $2^{n-1}$ even vertices of $Q^n$ induce an empty subgraph.
nodes.statement_short: The $2^{n-1}$ even-weight vertices form an independent set, so $2^{n-1}+1$ is the threshold.

nodes.name: Huang's induced subgraph theorem
nodes.statement: For every integer $n \ge 1$, let $H$ be an arbitrary $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph of $Q^n$, then $$\Delta(H) \ge \sqrt{n}.$$ Moreover this inequality is tight when $n$ is a perfect square.
assumptions: let $H$ be an arbitrary $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph of $Q^n$
let $H$ be an arbitrary $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph of $Q^n$

nodes.statement_short: Every induced subgraph of $Q^n$ on $2^{n-1}+1$ vertices has maximum degree $\ge\sqrt n$; tight for perfect squares.
nodes.label: thm_main

nodes.name: Tightness of the $\sqrt{n}$ bound for perfect squares
nodes.statement: Moreover this inequality is tight when $n$ is a perfect square.

nodes.name: Flipped vector $x^S$
nodes.statement: For $x \in \{0, 1\}^n$ and a subset $S$ of indices from $[n]=\{1, \cdots, n\}$, we denote by $x^S$ the binary vector obtained from $x$ by flipping all indices in $S$.

nodes.name: Sensitivity
nodes.statement: For $f: \{0, 1\}^n \rightarrow \{0, 1\}$, the {\it local sensitivity} $s(f, x)$ on the input $x$ is defined as the number of indices $i$, such that $f(x) \neq f(x^{\{i\}})$, and the {\it sensitivity} $s(f)$ of $f$ is $\max_{x} s(f, x)$.
nodes.statement_short: $s(f,x)$ = number of coordinates whose flip changes $f(x)$; $s(f)=\max_x s(f,x)$.

nodes.name: Local block sensitivity
nodes.statement: The {\it local block sensitivity} $bs(f, x)$ is the maximum number of disjoint blocks $B_1, \cdots, B_k$ of $[n]$, such that for each $B_i$, $f(x) \neq f(x^{B_i})$.
nodes.genus: maximum number of disjoint blocks $B_1, \cdots, B_k$ of $[n]$
nodes.statement_short: $bs(f,x)$ = maximum number of disjoint blocks of coordinates whose flip each changes $f(x)$.

nodes.name: Block sensitivity
nodes.statement: Similarly, the {\it block sensitivity} $bs(f)$ of $f$ is $\max_{x} bs(f, x)$.

nodes.name: Block sensitivity dominates sensitivity
nodes.statement: Obviously $bs(f) \ge s(f)$.

nodes.name: Sensitivity Conjecture
nodes.statement: (Sensitivity Conjecture) There exists an absolute constant $C>0$, such that for every boolean function $f$, $$bs(f) \le s(f)^C.$$
also_stated_at: A major open problem in complexity theory was posed by Nisan and Szegedy \cite{nisan-szegedy}, asking whether they are polynomially related.
nodes.statement_short: Block sensitivity is polynomially bounded by sensitivity: $bs(f)\le s(f)^C$ for an absolute $C$.

nodes.name: Polynomial equivalence of complexity measures with block sensitivity
nodes.statement: Although seemingly unnatural, the block sensitivity is known to be polynomially related to many other important complexity measures of boolean functions, including the decision tree complexity, the certificate complexity, the quantum and randomized query complexity, and the degree of the boolean function (as real polynomials), and the approximate degree \cite{survey}.
conclusions: the block sensitivity is known to be polynomially related to many other important complexity measures of boolean functions
nodes.statement_short: $bs(f)$ is polynomially related to decision-tree, certificate, quantum/randomized query complexity, degree and approximate degree.

nodes.name: Kenyon-Kutin exponential bound
nodes.statement: For example, Kenyon and Kutin \cite{kenyon-kutin} showed that $bs(f)=O(e^{s(f)}\sqrt{s(f)})$.

nodes.name: Rubinstein quadratic separation
nodes.statement: For the lower bound, Rubinstein \cite{rubinstein} first proposed a boolean function $f$ with $bs(f)=\frac{1}{2}s(f)^2$, showing a quadratic separation between these two complexity measures.
nodes.statement_short: There is a boolean function with $bs(f)=\frac12 s(f)^2$: a quadratic separation.

nodes.name: Complement subgraph $Q^n-H$
nodes.statement: For an induced graph $H$ of $Q^n$, let $Q^n-H$ denote the subgraph of $Q^n$ induced on the vertex set $V(Q^n) \setminus V(H)$.

nodes.name: $\Gamma(H)$
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma(H)=\max\{\Delta(H), \Delta(Q^n-H)\}$.

nodes.name: Degree of a boolean function
nodes.statement: The {\it degree} of a boolean function $f$, denoted by $\deg(f)$, is the degree of the unique multilinear real polynomial that represents $f$.
nodes.genus: degree of the unique multilinear real polynomial

nodes.name: Gotsman-Linial equivalence
nodes.statement: (Gotsman and Linial \cite{gotsman-linial}) The following are equivalent for any monotone function $h: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.\\ (a) For any induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ with $|V(H)|\neq 2^{n-1}$, we have $\Gamma(H) \ge h(n)$.\\ (b) For any boolean function $f$, we have $s(f) \ge h(\deg(f))$.
conclusions: The following are equivalent for any monotone function $h: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.\\ (a) For any induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ with $|V(H)|\neq 2^{n-1}$, we have $\Gamma(H) \ge h(n)$.\\ (b) For any boolean function $f$, we have $s(f) \ge h(\deg(f))$.
equivalent_conditions: (a) For any induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ with $|V(H)|\neq 2^{n-1}$, we have $\Gamma(H) \ge h(n)$.
(b) For any boolean function $f$, we have $s(f) \ge h(\deg(f))$.
nodes.statement_short: For monotone $h$: every unbalanced induced subgraph has $\Gamma(H)\ge h(n)$ iff every $f$ has $s(f)\ge h(\deg f)$.

nodes.name: Proof of $s(f) \ge \sqrt{\deg(f)}$
nodes.statement: Note that Theorem \ref{thm_main} implies that $h(n)$ can be taken as $\sqrt{n}$, since one of $H$ and $Q^n-H$ must contain at least $2^{n-1}+1$ vertices, and the maximum degree $\Delta$ is monotone.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.1 gives condition (a) of Gotsman-Linial with $h(n)=\sqrt n$ (one side has $\ge 2^{n-1}+1$ vertices); (b) follows.

nodes.name: Sensitivity-degree bound $s(f) \ge \sqrt{\deg(f)}$
nodes.statement: For every boolean function $f$, $$s(f) \ge \sqrt{\deg(f)}.$$

nodes.name: AND-of-ORs function attains $s(f)=\sqrt{\deg(f)}$
nodes.statement: This inequality is also tight for the AND-of-ORs boolean function \cite[Example 5.2]{survey}.

nodes.name: Nisan-Szegedy and Tal degree bounds
nodes.statement: Nisan and Szegedy \cite{nisan-szegedy} showed that $bs(f) \le 2 \deg(f)^2$ and this bound was later improved by Tal \cite{tal} to $bs(f) \le \deg(f)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Block sensitivity is at most quadratic in degree: $bs(f)\le 2\deg(f)^2$ (Nisan-Szegedy), improved to $\deg(f)^2$ (Tal).

nodes.name: Proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture ($bs \le s^4$)
nodes.statement: Combining these results we have confirmed the Sensitivity Conjecture.
nodes.statement_short: Chain $bs(f)\le\deg(f)^2\le s(f)^4$ (Tal's bound with Theorem 1.4).

nodes.name: Sensitivity Theorem $bs(f) \le s(f)^4$
nodes.statement: For every boolean function $f$, $$bs(f) \le s(f)^4.$$
nodes.label: thm_sensitivity

nodes.name: Principal submatrix
nodes.statement: Given a $n \times n$ matrix $A$, a {\it principal submatrix} of $A$ is obtained by deleting the same set of rows and columns from $A$.
differentia: obtained by deleting the same set of rows and columns from $A$

nodes.name: Cauchy's Interlace Theorem
nodes.statement: (Cauchy's Interlace Theorem) Let $A$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix, and $B$ be a $m \times m$ principal submatrix of $A$, for some $m<n$. If the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n$, and the eigenvalues of $B$ are $\mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge \cdots \ge \mu_m$, then for all $1 \le i \le m$, $$\lambda_i \ge \mu_i \ge \lambda_{i+n-m}.$$
assumptions: Let $A$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix, and $B$ be a $m \times m$ principal submatrix of $A$, for some $m<n$
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvalues of a principal $m\times m$ submatrix of a symmetric matrix interlace: $\lambda_i\ge\mu_i\ge\lambda_{i+n-m}$.
nodes.label: lem_cauchy

nodes.name: Proof pointer for Cauchy's Interlace Theorem
nodes.statement: Cauchy's Interlace Theorem is a direct consequence of the Courant-Fischer-Weyl min-max principle. A direct proof can also be found in \cite{fisk}.
nodes.statement_short: Not proved here: follows from the Courant-Fischer-Weyl min-max principle; a direct proof is in Fisk.

nodes.name: Signed hypercube matrix $A_n$ has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: We define a sequence of symmetric square matrices iteratively as follows, $$A_1=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},~~A_{n}=\begin{bmatrix} A_{n-1} & I \\ I & -A_{n-1} \end{bmatrix}.$$ Then $A_n$ is a $2^{n} \times 2^n$ matrix whose eigenvalues are $\sqrt{n}$ of multiplicity $2^{n-1}$, and $-\sqrt{n}$ of multiplicity $2^{n-1}$.
assumptions: We define a sequence of symmetric square matrices iteratively as follows, $$A_1=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},~~A_{n}=\begin{bmatrix} A_{n-1} & I \\ I & -A_{n-1} \end{bmatrix}.$$
conclusions: Then $A_n$ is a $2^{n} \times 2^n$ matrix whose eigenvalues are $\sqrt{n}$ of multiplicity $2^{n-1}$, and $-\sqrt{n}$ of multiplicity $2^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The recursively signed matrices $A_n$ ($2^n\times 2^n$) have eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt n$, each with multiplicity $2^{n-1}$.
nodes.label: lem_eig

nodes.name: Signed adjacency matrix $A_n$ of the hypercube
nodes.statement: We define a sequence of symmetric square matrices iteratively as follows, $$A_1=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},~~A_{n}=\begin{bmatrix} A_{n-1} & I \\ I & -A_{n-1} \end{bmatrix}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Recursive $\pm1$ signing of the hypercube adjacency matrix: $A_n=[[A_{n-1},I],[I,-A_{n-1}]]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: We prove by induction that $A_n^2=n I$. For $n=1$, $A_1^2=I$. Suppose the statement holds for $n-1$, that is $A_{n-1}^2=(n-1)I$, then $$A_n^2=\begin{bmatrix} A_{n-1}^2+I & 0 \\ 0 & A_{n-1}^2+I\end{bmatrix}=nI.$$ Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A_n$ are either $\sqrt{n}$ or $-\sqrt{n}$. Since $\mathrm{Tr}[A_n]=0$, we know that $A_n$ has exactly half of the eigenvalues being $\sqrt{n}$ and the rest being $-\sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ shows $A_n^2=nI$, so eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt n$; trace zero forces equal multiplicities.

nodes.name: Max degree bounds the top eigenvalue of a signed adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: Suppose $H$ is an $m$-vertex undirected graph, and $A$ is a symmetric matrix whose entries are in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and whose rows and columns are indexed by $V(H)$, and whenever $u$ and $v$ are non-adjacent in $H$, $A_{u,v}=0$. Then $$\Delta(H) \ge \lambda_1:=\lambda_1(A).$$
assumptions: $A$ is a symmetric matrix whose entries are in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and whose rows and columns are indexed by $V(H)$
nodes.statement_short: For any symmetric $\{-1,0,1\}$ matrix supported on the edges of $H$, $\Delta(H)\ge\lambda_1(A)$.
nodes.label: lem_key

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vec{v}$ is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1$. Then $\lambda_1 \vec{v} = A \vec{v}.$ Without loss of generality, assume $v_1$ is the coordinate of $\vec{v}$ that has the largest absolute value. Then $$|\lambda_1v_1| = |(A \vec{v})_1| = \left|\sum_{j=1}^m A_{1, j} v_j\right| = \left|\sum_{j \sim 1} A_{1, j} v_j \right| \le \sum_{j \sim 1} |A_{1, j}||v_1| \le \Delta(H) |v_1|.$$ Therefore $|\lambda_1| \le \Delta(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the top eigenvector, look at its largest coordinate, and bound $|\lambda_1 v_1|$ by the triangle inequality over the $\le\Delta(H)$ neighbours.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: Let $A_n$ be the sequence of matrices defined in Lemma \ref{lem_eig}. Note that the entries of $A_n$ are in $\{-1,0,1\}$. By the iterative construction of $A_n$, it is not hard to see that when changing every $(-1)$-entry of $A_n$ to $1$, we get exactly the adjacency matrix of $Q^n$, and thus $A_n$ and $Q^n$ satisfy the conditions in Lemma \ref{lem_key}. For example, we may let the upper-left and lower-right blocks of $A_n$ correspond to the two $(n-1)$-dimensional subcubes of $Q^n$, and the two identity blocks correspond to the perfect matching connecting these two subcubes. Therefore, a $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ and the principal submatrix $A_H$ of $A_{n}$ naturally induced by $H$ also satisfy the conditions of Lemma \ref{lem_key}. As a result, $$\Delta(H) \ge \lambda_1(A_H).$$ On the other hand, from Lemma \ref{lem_eig}, the eigenvalues of $A_n$ are known to be $$\sqrt{n}, \cdots, \sqrt{n}, -\sqrt{n}, \cdots, -\sqrt{n}.$$ Note that $A_H$ is a $(2^{n-1}+1) \times (2^{n-1}+1)$ submatrix of the $2^n \times 2^n$ matrix $A_n$. By Cauchy's Interlace Theorem, $$\lambda_1(A_H) \ge \lambda_{2^{n-1}}(A_n)=\sqrt{n}.$$ Combining the two inequalities we just obtained, we have $\Delta(H) \ge \sqrt{n},$ completing the proof of our theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the signed matrix $A_n$ to $H$: Lemma 2.3 gives $\Delta(H)\ge\lambda_1(A_H)$, and Cauchy interlacing with Lemma 2.2 gives $\lambda_1(A_H)\ge\sqrt n$.

nodes.name: Spectral strengthening and its tightness
nodes.statement: From the proof, one actually has $\lambda_1(H) \ge \lambda_1(A_H) \ge \sqrt{n}$. Since $\Delta(H) \ge \lambda_1(H)$, this result strengthens Theorem \ref{thm_main}. More interestingly, the inequality $\lambda_1(H) \ge \sqrt{n}$ is best possible for all $n$. This can be seen by taking all the even vertices and one odd vertex of $Q^n$, then the induced subgraph is a copy of the star $K_{1, n}$, together with many isolated vertices. The largest eigenvalue of this induced subgraph is exactly $\sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The proof gives $\lambda_1(H)\ge\sqrt n$, stronger than Theorem 1.1 and tight for every $n$ (a star $K_{1,n}$).

nodes.name: Spectral strengthening $\lambda_1(H) \ge \sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: From the proof, one actually has $\lambda_1(H) \ge \lambda_1(A_H) \ge \sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: $\lambda_1(H) \ge \sqrt{n}$ is best possible
nodes.statement: More interestingly, the inequality $\lambda_1(H) \ge \sqrt{n}$ is best possible for all $n$.
conclusions: the inequality $\lambda_1(H) \ge \sqrt{n}$ is best possible for all $n$

nodes.name: Star construction showing tightness
nodes.statement: This can be seen by taking all the even vertices and one odd vertex of $Q^n$, then the induced subgraph is a copy of the star $K_{1, n}$, together with many isolated vertices. The largest eigenvalue of this induced subgraph is exactly $\sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Even vertices plus one odd vertex induce a star $K_{1,n}$ plus isolated vertices, whose top eigenvalue is $\sqrt n$.

nodes.name: Induced subgraphs on $\alpha(G)+1$ vertices of symmetric graphs
nodes.statement: Given a ``nice'' graph $G$ with high symmetry, denote by $\alpha(G)$ its independence number. Let $f(G)$ be the minimum of the maximum degree of an induced subgraph of $G$ on $\alpha(G)+1$ vertices. What can we say about $f(G)$? In particular, for which graphs, the method used in proving Theorem \ref{thm_main} would provide a tight bound?
nodes.statement_short: For symmetric graphs $G$, how small can the max degree of an induced subgraph on $\alpha(G)+1$ vertices be, and when is the spectral method tight?

nodes.name: Asymptotics of $g(n,k)$ for the hypercube
nodes.statement: Back to the hypercube problem, let $g(n, k)$ be the minimum $t$, such that every $t$-vertex induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ has maximum degree at least $k$. In this paper, we show that $g(n, \sqrt{n}) = 2^{n-1}+1$. It would be interesting to determine $g(n, k)$ asymptotically for other values of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the minimum size $g(n,k)$ forcing max degree $\ge k$ in induced subgraphs of $Q^n$, for $k\ne\sqrt n$.

nodes.name: Ambainis-Sun quadratic separation
nodes.statement: Although we have shown a tight bound between the sensitivity and the degree, at the time of writing this paper, the best separation between the block sensitivity $bs(f)$ and the sensitivity $s(f)$ is $bs(f)=\frac{2}{3}s(f)^2-\frac{1}{3}s(f)$ shown in \cite{ambainis-sun}, which is quadratic.
nodes.statement_short: Best known separation: functions with $bs(f)=\frac23 s(f)^2-\frac13 s(f)$.

nodes.name: Close the quadratic-quartic gap between $bs$ and $s$
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm_sensitivity} only shows a quartic upper bound. Perhaps one could close this gap by directly applying the spectral method to boolean functions instead of to the hypercubes.
nodes.statement_short: Is $bs(f)=O(s(f)^2)$? Close the gap between the quadratic separation and the quartic upper bound, perhaps spectrally on $f$ directly.

nodes.name: Set up induction
nodes.statement: We prove by induction that $A_n^2=n I$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $A_n^2=nI$ by induction on $n$

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement_short: Base case $n=1$

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose the statement holds for $n-1$, that is $A_{n-1}^2=(n-1)I$, then $$A_n^2=\begin{bmatrix} A_{n-1}^2+I & 0 \\ 0 & A_{n-1}^2+I\end{bmatrix}=nI.$$
nodes.statement_short: Block multiplication: off-diagonal blocks cancel, diagonal blocks give $(n-1)I+I$

nodes.name: Eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A_n$ are either $\sqrt{n}$ or $-\sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: $A_n^2=nI$ forces every eigenvalue to be $\pm\sqrt n$

nodes.name: Trace zero gives equal multiplicities
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{Tr}[A_n]=0$, we know that $A_n$ has exactly half of the eigenvalues being $\sqrt{n}$ and the rest being $-\sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Trace zero splits the spectrum evenly

nodes.name: Top eigenvector
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vec{v}$ is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1$. Then $\lambda_1 \vec{v} = A \vec{v}.$
nodes.statement_short: Take the eigenvector of $\lambda_1$

nodes.name: WLOG largest coordinate
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, assume $v_1$ is the coordinate of $\vec{v}$ that has the largest absolute value.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $v_1$ has the largest absolute value

nodes.name: Triangle inequality over neighbours
nodes.statement: Then $$|\lambda_1v_1| = |(A \vec{v})_1| = \left|\sum_{j=1}^m A_{1, j} v_j\right| = \left|\sum_{j \sim 1} A_{1, j} v_j \right| \le \sum_{j \sim 1} |A_{1, j}||v_1| \le \Delta(H) |v_1|.$$
nodes.statement_short: Only neighbours contribute; bound by $\Delta(H)|v_1|$

nodes.name: Conclude $|\lambda_1| \le \Delta(H)$
nodes.statement: Therefore $|\lambda_1| \le \Delta(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $|v_1|$

nodes.name: Take the signed matrices $A_n$
nodes.statement: Let $A_n$ be the sequence of matrices defined in Lemma \ref{lem_eig}. Note that the entries of $A_n$ are in $\{-1,0,1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the matrices of Lemma 2.2, with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$

nodes.name: $A_n$ is a signing of the adjacency matrix of $Q^n$
nodes.statement: By the iterative construction of $A_n$, it is not hard to see that when changing every $(-1)$-entry of $A_n$ to $1$, we get exactly the adjacency matrix of $Q^n$, and thus $A_n$ and $Q^n$ satisfy the conditions in Lemma \ref{lem_key}. For example, we may let the upper-left and lower-right blocks of $A_n$ correspond to the two $(n-1)$-dimensional subcubes of $Q^n$, and the two identity blocks correspond to the perfect matching connecting these two subcubes.
nodes.statement_short: Unsigning $A_n$ gives the adjacency matrix of $Q^n$ (two subcubes plus a matching), so Lemma 2.3 applies

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.3 to the restriction $A_H$
nodes.statement: Therefore, a $(2^{n-1}+1)$-vertex induced subgraph $H$ of $Q^n$ and the principal submatrix $A_H$ of $A_{n}$ naturally induced by $H$ also satisfy the conditions of Lemma \ref{lem_key}. As a result, $$\Delta(H) \ge \lambda_1(A_H).$$
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to $H$ and apply Lemma 2.3: $\Delta(H)\ge\lambda_1(A_H)$

nodes.name: Spectrum of $A_n$ from Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: On the other hand, from Lemma \ref{lem_eig}, the eigenvalues of $A_n$ are known to be $$\sqrt{n}, \cdots, \sqrt{n}, -\sqrt{n}, \cdots, -\sqrt{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Recall the spectrum $\pm\sqrt n$ of $A_n$

nodes.name: Cauchy interlacing
nodes.statement: Note that $A_H$ is a $(2^{n-1}+1) \times (2^{n-1}+1)$ submatrix of the $2^n \times 2^n$ matrix $A_n$. By Cauchy's Interlace Theorem, $$\lambda_1(A_H) \ge \lambda_{2^{n-1}}(A_n)=\sqrt{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Interlacing for the $(2^{n-1}+1)$-principal submatrix gives $\lambda_1(A_H)\ge\lambda_{2^{n-1}}(A_n)=\sqrt n$

nodes.name: Combine the two inequalities
nodes.statement: Combining the two inequalities we just obtained, we have $\Delta(H) \ge \sqrt{n},$ completing the proof of our theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two bounds: $\Delta(H)\ge\sqrt n$
